subject: Reception and display joinery
hook: Your reception desk is the first handshake. Brief it properly.
ig:
Your reception desk is the first handshake a visitor gets. It's worth briefing properly before anyone draws it.

January is when a lot of offices, salons and clinics plan their refresh. If a new reception desk is on the list, these are the decisions that shape the design:

How many staff work behind it at the busiest time.
The two heights: a standing-height ledge for visitors, a seated-height worktop for staff.
An accessible lowered section so nobody has to talk up at the counter.
Where power and data come in for screens, phones and card readers.
A front finish that copes with bags, feet and cleaning.

Get these right and the joinery does its job quietly for years. Get them wrong and staff end up working around the desk instead of at it.

Save this for your office refit, and find our commercial cabinet making via the link in bio.

on_asset: S1: Your reception desk is the first handshake | 6 decisions to make before design | S2: Who sits there, and how many — One person or two at peak times changes the length, the knee space and how much storage sits behind the counter. | S3: Two heights, two jobs — A raised ledge at standing height for visitors to lean and sign; a lower worktop at seated height for the person working behind it. | S4: Make one section accessible — A lowered stretch of counter lets wheelchair users and children talk across the desk face to face, not up at it. | S5: Plan power and data early — Screens, card readers, phones and printers all need a socket and a cable route. Mark the floor and wall points before the desk is drawn. | S6: Pick a finish for heavy traffic — The front gets kicked by bags and feet. Choose a hard-wearing board and edge, and keep the brand colour where it's seen, not scuffed. | S7: Save for your office refit | Staff, heights, access, power, finish.
